title: The Teacher's Work Is Like the Landscape
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In this reflective, letter-style post addressed to colleague, Stuart uses a walk through an icy winter prairie as an extended metaphor for the invisible, slow-building impact of teaching. He describes seeing flashing glimpses of the landscape's other seasons layered beneath the frozen ground and uses that image to argue that a wintry, discouraging stretch of the school year doesn't mean growth and connection have stopped happening, only that a teacher, as a finite creature, can't always see the results of their work in real time. The piece is explicitly aimed at teachers going through a hard season, reassuring them that it's possible to see no results for months but still be doing something important. It reads as pastoral encouragement rather than instructional advice, part of Stuart's recurring practice of writing personal, morale-sustaining reflections to his teacher audience.
points: Uses the metaphor of dormant winter prairie concealing the first shoots of spring as an argument that invisible, cumulative teacher impact is real even when it can't be observed in the moment.
Explicitly names the limits of a teacher's perspective — Omniscience is not our place in the cosmos — as a reason to trust the process rather than demand visible proof of progress.
Ties encouragement to concrete outcomes he asserts are happening beneath the surface: mastery has grown, learning has taken place, and connection has altered life trajectories.
Positions the reflection explicitly as morale-boosting for a specific hard moment (weather cancellations, a difficult trimester) rather than as a general instructional strategy.
quotes: I've taken a dozen or so walks these past couple of weeks because, when I'm in the valley, sometimes that's all I can do. Walking stabilizes my soul; it depressurizes me.

As I walked and felt the cold sinking in to me, I started seeing the landscape as it has appeared to me in other seasons. Beneath the ice and within the dormant plants there has been, and will be again, the first shoots of spring, the flourishing of summer, and the quiet, regalness of fall.

No matter how wintry your practice has felt this school year, colleague, reflect on how it has also housed the spring. Mastery has grown. Learning has taken place. And connection has done what connection does: alter life trajectories, for the better.
But, as a finite creature fixed in time, you may see none of it right now. We just don't get to see it all. Omniscience is not our place in the cosmos.
It's possible to see no results for months but still to be doing something important.
